Personalised exercise programme
No needles, no lab tests, no genetic tests. The way you move says a lot about how long, and how well, you will live.
I measure these markers in your home, work out your functional age and turn the results into an exercise prescription made for you.
16% Grip strength Higher risk of death for every 5 kg drop, a stronger marker than blood pressure. Lancet 2015 · 139,691 people
12% Walking speed Lower risk of death for every 0.1 m/s faster walking speed. JAMA 2011 · 34,485 people
84% One-leg balance Higher risk of death in people who can’t stand on one leg for 10 seconds. BJSM 2022 · 1,702 people
6 times Rising from the floor Higher risk of cardiovascular death with a low score on the sitting-rising test. Eur J Prev Cardiol 2026 · 4,282 people
Measured, not guessed. Every indicator is backed by a published study, and you keep your results as a written report.
The good news: you can’t change your genes, but you can improve your strength, balance and walking at any age.

What’s your real age?
Four simple tests you can do at home in 2–3 minutes: muscle strength, balance, daily activity and fitness.
Do the tests next to a sturdy chair and a wall or table you can hold on to.
Stop straight away if you feel dizzy, have chest pain or become short of breath.
If you have heart disease, skip the stair test.

Sit on a sturdy chair with its back against a wall, arms crossed over your chest. Without using your arms, stand up fully and sit back down 5 times, as fast as you can. You can use the stopwatch below.
Stand next to a wall with your arms by your sides, looking straight ahead. Rest the toes of the lifted foot against the back of your other calf. You have 3 attempts on each foot.
Check last week’s average in your phone’s health app. If you don’t know, estimate: a brisk 30-minute walk is about 3,000–4,000 steps.
About 60 steps, without stopping: quickly, but without running. If you haven’t tried recently, choose your best estimate.
If you have heart disease, chest pain or shortness of breath, don’t do this test; choose the “I haven’t tried” option.

This test does not diagnose anything; it is for information only and gives a rough estimate. An accurate assessment comes from a detailed analysis that measures strength, power, balance, gait and flexibility.

Brain, spine and a three-armed Y
My registered logo represents my professional journey and my holistic view of recovery.
Tap the numbers to explore each part of the logo.
Brain

The brain, which forms the main shape of the logo, expresses the importance of neuroscience, mental processes and mental training in recovery. The brain is not just a centre that directs the body; it also plays an important part in how pain is perceived, in relearning movement, in motivation and in adapting to the recovery process.
That is why I see mental training and neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change, as an inseparable part of physical recovery.
Spine

The spine at the centre of the brain symbolises the body’s main load-bearing axis, posture, movement, balance and the neural communication between brain and body. It also draws inspiration from manual therapy approaches built around the spine, such as osteopathy and chiropractic.
The three arms of the Y

Besides the two universities where I studied, the three arms of the “Y” in the logo represent three valued scientists who mentored me in my professional development, trained me, and in whose clinical studies I worked as an assistant:
Prof. Dr. Nezih Hekim
Prof. Dr. Kemal Nuri Özerkan
Prof. Dr. Cihan Aksoy
Two Ys and the colour blend
The two “Y” shapes and the way their colours blend into each other express the philosophy of Yin–Yang: the complementary sides of Eastern and Western medicine.
The yellow tone: Healing is voltage

The yellow tone of the Y, reminiscent of electricity, refers to the body’s electrical and biological communication processes. It brings electrotherapy from physiotherapy together with acupuncture and dry needling from medicine around one scientific question: how do these methods act through the body’s electricity? It stands for my research into that question, and for a new scientific perspective that might one day reach as far as a Nobel Prize.
12 vertebrae and Lambda λ
The 12 vertebrae in the logo symbolise Lambda (λ), Book 12 of Aristotle’s Metaphysics . Turned upside down, the Lambda sign comes close to the “Y” shape and joins the logo’s other meanings.

In short, my logo represents the unity of brain and body, the central role of the spine, the union of mental, physical and spiritual healing, the synthesis of East and West, and the three valued mentors who have guided my scientific journey.

p.t: What can you do in stressful moments?
p.d: Five skills adapted from a World Health Organization guide, breathing exercises (4-6, box, 4-7-8) and a free illustrated guide with audio exercises.
s: Five skills that take a few minutes a day, adapted from the illustrated guide the World Health Organization wrote for everyone, plus a breathing exercise.
Breathing exercise

Slowing your breathing helps your body calm down. Sit somewhere comfortable and let your shoulders drop. Breathe in through your nose as the circle grows and breathe out slowly as it shrinks. When the edge of the circle turns gold, hold your breath.
Breathe in for 4 seconds and out for 6. No holding. Keep going for as long as you like.
One round takes 10 seconds. 6 rounds take about 1 minute.

Do the holds without straining. If you feel dizzy or short of breath, switch to the Calm pace or return to your normal breathing. If you have serious heart or lung disease, ask your doctor before using techniques with breath holds.
A calm, classical start to the week
To turn inward over a cup of coffee: a Spotify playlist of Ludovico Einaudi’s Nuvole Bianche and similar calm piano pieces. You can play it in the background before or after the breathing exercise.
Small tools for hard moments
These skills are not meant to make stress disappear completely. The aim is to stay grounded even when difficult feelings are there, and to be able to turn back to what matters to you.

1 Ground yourself When emotions come like a storm, it is like dropping anchor until the storm passes. Notice Quietly notice what you are thinking and feeling right now. Your body Press your feet into the floor, straighten your back, breathe out slowly and stretch your shoulders. Look around Notice, one by one, the things you can see, hear and touch around you. Then go back to what you were doing.

2 Unhook from difficult thoughts Difficult thoughts can catch us like a fishing hook and pull us away from the life we are living right now. Notice Notice that a thought has hooked you. Name it Say to yourself: “I’m noticing a difficult thought.” Refocus Bring your attention back to what you are doing and to the people around you.

3 Act on your values We cannot always change our circumstances, but we can choose the kind of person we want to be. What matters to you: being patient, kind, helpful? This week Choose a small, doable step that shows this value, such as calling a friend or helping a neighbour.

4 Be kind to yourself Treat yourself the way you would treat a friend who is going through a hard time. Touch Gently place a hand on your chest and feel its warmth. Say “This is really hard. I am not alone in feeling this way.”

5 Make room for feelings Fighting a difficult feeling often makes it bigger. Try carrying it with you for a while instead. Be curious Where in your body do you feel the emotion? If it were an object, what would its shape, colour and temperature be? Breathe out Breathe out slowly around that area and make room for it. Feelings come and go.
Frequently asked questions
How do you do a breathing exercise when you are stressed?

Sit somewhere comfortable and let your shoulders drop. Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds and out slowly over 6 seconds. One round takes 10 seconds; 6 rounds take about 1 minute. Slowing your breathing helps your body calm down.
How do you do box breathing and 4-7-8 breathing?

For box breathing, breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 4, breathe out for 4 and hold for 4. For the 4-7-8 technique, breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds, hold for 7, then breathe out through slightly parted lips over 8 seconds. Do the holds without straining; if you have serious heart or lung disease, ask your doctor before using techniques with breath holds.
What are the five skills in the World Health Organization’s stress guide?

Grounding yourself, unhooking from difficult thoughts, acting on your values, being kind to yourself and making room for feelings. The aim is not to make stress disappear completely, but to be able to turn back to what matters to you even when difficult feelings are there.
Illustrated guide and audio exercises
You can get the full guide and its audio exercises free of charge from the World Health Organization. The audio recordings are available in more than 20 languages, including English.

Light, a mirror and ice: the 2026 Nobel Prizes

The medicine prize went to three pioneers of optogenetics, which lets brain cells be switched on and off with light; the chemistry prize to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who showed how to make only one of two mirror-image molecules; and the physics prize to Francis Halzen, who caught cosmic neutrinos in the ice of the South Pole.

All three began with a curiosity that looked useless at the time: a pond alga, a reaction that did not add up, and a flash of light at the bottom of the ice. I have explained all three in plain language, with animations.
Sources: STAT, 5 October 2026 · IceCube, 6 October 2026 · Forbes, 7 October 2026
Open the animated explainer →
More blood tests for Alzheimer's

Since May 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved four tests that measure amyloid and tau changes in the brain from a blood sample. The latest two arrived in August 2026. These tests may make diagnosis easier, without the need for brain imaging or a lumbar puncture to collect spinal fluid.
Important: the tests are approved only for use in people with memory complaints, as part of an assessment by a doctor. They are not suitable for screening healthy people who have no symptoms.
Source: TIME, 22 September 2026
A pig kidney became a bridge to a human kidney

In the US, Tim Andrews, 66, who had end-stage kidney failure, received a kidney from a gene-edited pig. The kidney kept him off dialysis for 271 days, the longest period documented in a living recipient. When his immunosuppressive drugs were reduced because of an infection, the pig kidney was damaged and stopped working; in January 2026 Andrews received a human kidney from a donor, which started working straight away.

Given how long organ waiting lists are, this is a hopeful step. For now, though, experience comes from only a small number of patients; the safety and durability of gene-edited pig kidneys are being studied in clinical trials.
Sources: The Lancet, 9 September 2026 · Mass General Brigham
First gene therapy for Huntington's disease awaits approval

Huntington's disease is an inherited, progressive brain disease that affects movement, thinking and mood, and no treatment has been proven to slow its course. AMT-130, developed by uniQure, is delivered in a one-off, MRI-guided operation to the striatum, an area deep in the brain, and aims to reduce production of the faulty huntingtin protein that causes the disease. In patients who received the high dose, the disease progressed 75% more slowly at year 3 than in a comparison group; the company applied for approval in the US and the UK in September 2026.

The results are based on a small number of patients and on a comparison with similar patients selected from disease registries rather than a placebo group. In the year 4 data released on 29 September, the difference on the main rating scale shrank to 44% and was not statistically significant, while a 61% slowing held up on a scale of daily functioning. Of those who received the high dose, 17% had a serious side effect linked to inflammation in the brain; all of these events resolved.
Sources: uniQure, 29 September 2026 · BioPharm International, 2 September 2026
A Parkinson's drug that works in a new way: tavapadon

On 28 September 2026, the FDA approved AbbVie's drug tavapadon (JUVMO). Taken as a tablet once a day, it is the first drug to selectively stimulate D1 and D5, two of the dopamine receptors in the brain; the dopamine agonists used today act mainly on D2 and D3 receptors. It can be used on its own or together with levodopa. In patients taking levodopa, it increased “on” time, the good periods without troublesome involuntary movements, by 1.7 hours a day; with placebo the increase was 0.6 hours.

The most common side effects are nausea, headache, taste disturbance, tiredness and dizziness; care is needed because of the risk of a drop in blood pressure on standing, hallucinations and impulse-control problems such as compulsive gambling. Although new drugs can make movement easier, regular exercise remains a core part of treatment for Parkinson's disease.
Source: AbbVie, 28 September 2026
Parkinson's disease guide →
First drug to replace the missing brain signal in type 1 narcolepsy

In type 1 narcolepsy, the brain loses the cells that make orexin (hypocretin), a substance that regulates wakefulness. People struggle with irresistible sleep attacks during the day, and their muscles can suddenly go weak when they laugh or get excited (cataplexy). On 5 August 2026, the FDA approved Takeda's drug oveporexton (Orzeyful) as the first drug to stand in for the missing orexin signal. In two studies involving 273 patients, daytime wakefulness improved, and sleepiness and cataplexy attacks fell markedly.

According to the FDA, it is the first drug to act on the underlying biology of the disease. It is taken twice a day; the most common side effects are difficulty sleeping, needing to pass urine often and increased saliva. Its safety and effectiveness in people under 18 are not yet known.
Source: FDA, 5 August 2026
Pancreatic cancer gets its first RAS-blocking drug

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers carry a mutation in the RAS genes (usually KRAS) that drive tumour growth. RAS was long thought impossible to target with drugs; medicines aimed at just one specific RAS mutation were already used in lung and bowel cancer, while daraxonrasib (Rasonque), which blocks many forms of RAS at once, received FDA approval on 26 August 2026. In the RASolute 302 study of 500 patients whose pancreatic cancer had spread and who had already been treated, median survival was 6.7 months with chemotherapy and 13.2 months with daraxonrasib.

It is taken as a tablet once a day. The most common side effects are rash, diarrhoea, mouth sores and nausea. One oncologist quoted by STAT called it the biggest advance in pancreatic cancer in decades; studies of the drug as first-line treatment are ongoing.
Sources: FDA, 26 August 2026 · STAT
Personalised mRNA cancer vaccine succeeds in phase III for the first time

Intismeran, developed by Merck and Moderna, is an mRNA vaccine made individually for each patient, based on the mutations in their tumour. In the INTerpath-001 study of 1,137 patients with stage IIB–IV melanoma whose tumour had been completely removed by surgery, the vaccine was given together with an immunotherapy drug (pembrolizumab) and delayed the return of the disease and its spread to distant organs compared with the drug alone.

Detailed figures have not yet been released; the results will be presented at a medical congress. In the earlier phase IIb study, the risk of recurrence or death was 49% lower. No new safety concerns were seen.
Sources: Merck, 19 August 2026 · STAT
Stem cell–derived brain cell transplants in Parkinson’s

In the STEM-PD study, led by Lund University in Sweden and the University of Cambridge in the UK, dopamine-producing cells made from stem cells were transplanted into the brains of 8 people with moderate Parkinson’s disease. Of the 7 patients assessed after one year, 6 substantially reduced their medication dose, and brain scans suggested that the transplanted cells had survived.

No serious side effects were linked to the cells. Because this was a small, early-phase study, longer follow-up and larger studies are needed to see whether the effect lasts; the treatment is not yet in routine use.
Sources: Nature Medicine, 9 July 2026 · Parkinson’s UK
A drug “shuttled” into the brain: trontinemab

Trontinemab, developed by Roche, is designed to cross the blood–brain barrier more easily with the help of a carrier. According to early-phase data presented at the AAIC Alzheimer's conference in July 2026, amyloid build-up in the brain fell below the threshold level at 28 weeks in 92% of patients who received the high dose.
The drug is not yet approved; large phase III trials are ongoing. Side effects such as microbleeds in the brain were seen in a small number of patients.
Source: Clinical Trials Arena, 16 July 2026
The first PCSK9 pill for cholesterol

PCSK9 drugs lower 'bad' (LDL) cholesterol powerfully, but until now they have only been available as injections. On 17 July 2026, the FDA approved Merck's drug enlicitide (Lipfendra) as the first PCSK9 pill, taken once a day. In two trials involving a total of 3,207 people already taking statins, LDL cholesterol at week 24 fell by 56% more than with placebo in people with, or at high risk of, cardiovascular disease, and by 59% more in people with familial hypercholesterolaemia.
It is approved for use alongside diet and exercise. The outcome study that will show whether it reduces heart attacks and strokes has not yet been completed.
Source: FDA, 17 July 2026
CAR-T cell therapy for severe lupus

CAR-T, a method used to treat cancer, is also being tried in diseases where the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. In the CARLYSLE study run by University College London (UCL), immune cells from people with severe lupus were reprogrammed to target the B cells that drive the disease. In the lower-dose group, 5 of 6 patients went into remission by standard criteria, and those with kidney involvement lost less protein in their urine.

There was no severe cytokine release syndrome and no nervous system side effects; liver injury in one patient resolved completely. These results come from an early study of 9 patients; a larger phase II study has started recruiting in the UK.
Source: UCL, 12 June 2026
Blocking small arteries for knee osteoarthritis pain (GAE)

At Charité University Hospital in Berlin, 194 patients whose osteoarthritis pain had not improved with other treatments for at least 3 months had genicular artery embolisation: a thin catheter was used to deliver microspheres, which dissolve within a few hours, into small arteries around the knee. Median pain fell from 7 out of 10 to 3 at 12 months, and 80% of patients improved meaningfully.

There were no moderate or severe side effects. However, this was a single-centre study without a control group, and only 79% of patients could be reached at 12 months. Exercise remains the cornerstone of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
Source: Radiology, 16 June 2026 · ScienceDaily
Knee osteoarthritis guide →
Catching many cancers early with a single blood test: the first major results

The NHS-Galleri study in England included 142,942 people aged 50–77 with no symptoms. Half of them had the Galleri test once a year for 3 years; the test looks in the blood for fragments of DNA shed by tumours. In the test group, about 4 times as many cancers were picked up by screening; diagnoses of stage IV cancer (cancer that has spread) fell by 14%, and more cancers were caught at an earlier stage.

The study did not achieve a significant reduction in stage III–IV cancers, which was its main goal. It is not yet known whether earlier diagnosis helps people live longer. This test does not replace breast, cervical and bowel cancer screening.
Sources: ASCO, June 2026 · The ASCO Post
New weight-loss drug also eased knee osteoarthritis pain

Retatrutide, developed by Eli Lilly, is a once-weekly injection that stimulates three hormone receptors involved in appetite and metabolism (GLP-1, GIP and glucagon) at the same time. In the TRIUMPH-4 study of 445 people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis, those on the highest dose lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight over 68 weeks; knee pain fell by 74–76% on the two doses, compared with 40.3% in the placebo group. In the TRIUMPH-1 study of 2,339 people, announced in June 2026, pain also fell by up to 73% in participants with knee osteoarthritis, although it is worth remembering that pain also fell by 40% on placebo in TRIUMPH-4.

Retatrutide is not yet approved and is used only in clinical trials; products sold online as “retatrutide” are illegal and cannot be trusted. Nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting were common; at the highest dose, about 18% of patients stopped the drug because of side effects. In knee osteoarthritis, combining weight loss with strengthening exercises remains important.
Sources: Eli Lilly, 11 December 2025 · Eli Lilly, 6 June 2026
A new class of drug for hard-to-control blood pressure

In people whose blood pressure stays high despite taking several medicines, the hormone aldosterone, which makes the body hold on to salt and water, plays an important part. AstraZeneca's drug baxdrostat (Baxfendy) received FDA approval in May 2026 as the first drug to selectively block aldosterone synthase, the enzyme that makes aldosterone. In the BaxHTN study of 796 patients taking at least two blood pressure medicines, systolic blood pressure fell by 8.7–9.8 mmHg more than with placebo at 12 weeks.

The main side effect to watch for is a rise in potassium in the blood: potassium above 6.0 mmol/L occurred in 3% of people on the high dose and 0.4% on placebo, so potassium levels are monitored with blood tests. Do not change your blood pressure medicine without talking to your doctor. Alongside medicines, regular exercise, especially isometric exercise, has also been shown to lower blood pressure.
Sources: New England Journal of Medicine, 2025 · Pharmacy Times, May 2026
Wall sits for blood pressure →
The first GLP-1 weight-loss pill with no food or water restrictions

Until now, GLP-1 drugs have mostly been used as weekly injections, while oral semaglutide (the Wegovy pill), approved in December 2025, has to be taken on an empty stomach. On 1 April 2026, the FDA approved Eli Lilly's orforglipron (Foundayo) as the first GLP-1 pill that can be taken at any time of day, with no food or water restrictions. In the 72-week ATTAIN-1 study, those on the highest dose lost an average of 12.4% of their body weight, compared with 0.9% on placebo.

It is approved for use together with a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. Nausea, constipation and diarrhoea are common, and the warnings about thyroid tumour risk, pancreatitis and gallbladder problems apply to this drug too. Strengthening exercises are important to reduce muscle loss while you lose weight.
Source: Eli Lilly, 1 April 2026
How much activity is enough? →
Chronic low back pain: which treatment should you start with?

In the US OPTIMIZE study of 749 people with chronic low back pain, participants first received 8 weeks of physiotherapy or cognitive behavioural therapy; those who did not benefit enough switched treatments or moved to a mindfulness programme. At week 10, those who started with physiotherapy had slightly better day-to-day function, while pain levels were similar between the groups.

Although the gains were modest, physiotherapy emerged as a reasonable first step. After one year there was no meaningful difference between the second-stage options; switching or adding treatments later made little difference to the long-term outcome.
Source: Annals of Internal Medicine, 20 April 2026
Low back pain guide →
Gene therapy for inherited deafness appears to last

42 people aged 9 months to 32 years with hearing loss caused by a fault in the OTOF gene had a harmless, modified virus carrying a healthy copy of the gene placed in the inner ear. In the study, run at eight centres in China, 90% of participants had better hearing at 2.5 years of follow-up, and more than half reached normal hearing levels. Children progressed from responding to sounds to speaking in short sentences and even singing.

There were no serious side effects. The effect was strongest in people aged 18 and under; 10% of participants did not respond. The treatment is only for OTOF-related hearing loss, and the approval process is just beginning.
Source: Nature, 22 April 2026 · Harvard Gazette
Fast typing at home with a brain–computer interface

In the US BrainGate study, small electrodes were placed in the movement area of the brain of two participants, one with advanced ALS and one with a spinal cord injury at neck level. The system turned attempted finger movements into letters on a keyboard. One participant typed 22 words a minute in their own home with a word error rate of just 1.6%, and about 30 sentences were enough to set the system up.
A big step in communication for people who cannot speak or use their hands. The device is still for research use only and requires brain surgery.
Source: Nature Neuroscience · Brown University, 16 March 2026
Electrical stimulation after spinal cord injury: hope and reality

In a small study at Brown University in the US, 3 people with complete spinal cord injury had electrodes placed below and above the injury. Stimulation below the injury activated the leg muscles, while stimulation above it gave feedback on knee angle and stepping through signals felt in the chest, arm or back; the participants walked on a treadmill with a harness and a therapist’s support. In the international eWALK study of 48 people, however, stimulation delivered through the skin gave no extra benefit on top of 12 weeks of walking training.

The main message of eWALK: walking training on its own clearly improved walking, even in people who had lived with a spinal cord injury for a long time. Stimulation technologies are promising, but they do not yet replace rehabilitation.
Sources: Brown University, 11 March 2026 · eClinicalMedicine, 2026
AI support in mammography: results of the first randomised trial

In the MASAI study of more than 105,000 women in Sweden, mammograms were read either with AI support or in the standard way by two radiologists. In the AI-supported group, 81% of cancers were caught at screening (74% in the standard group); there were 12% fewer cancers found between screening rounds and 27% fewer cancers of aggressive subtypes. False alarm rates were similar in both groups.

AI is not replacing the radiologist but supporting them; interim results had shown a 44% reduction in radiologists’ reading workload. The study was done in a single country, with one device and one software system, and with experienced radiologists.
Sources: The Lancet, 29 January 2026 · EurekAlert!
Changing the way you walk in knee osteoarthritis

In a study of 68 people with osteoarthritis on the inner side of the knee, run by researchers from the University of Utah, New York University and Stanford University in the US, motion analysis was used to decide for each participant whether turning the toes 5 or 10 degrees inwards or outwards would help more, followed by 6 sessions of gait training. Over one year, pain fell by an average of 2.5 points out of 10 (1.3 in the sham training group). MRI findings suggested that cartilage breakdown progressed more slowly.
This is not a one-size-fits-all tip like “turn your toes in”; it needs individual measurement and expert guidance. The measurement will need to be simplified before the method can be widely used.
Source: The Lancet Rheumatology, October 2025
Exercise after colon cancer saves lives

In the CHALLENGE study of 889 people with colon cancer in 6 countries who had finished chemotherapy, one group joined a 3-year, coach-supported, personalised exercise programme (from brisk walking to group classes); the other group received health education only. At 5 years, 80% of the exercise group and 74% of the other group were cancer-free; at 8 years, survival was 90% versus 83%.

In the exercise group, the risk of cancer returning, a new cancer or death was 28% lower, and the risk of death 37% lower. It is the first large randomised trial to show that exercise can be part of cancer treatment.
Sources: New England Journal of Medicine, June 2025 · Oncology Central
Insulin-producing cells made from stem cells for type 1 diabetes

Zimislecel, developed by Vertex, consists of insulin-producing islet cells grown in the laboratory from stem cells. Of 12 patients who received the full dose, 10 no longer needed insulin injections after one year; all 12 had an HbA1c below 7% and no severe low blood sugar episodes.
Immunosuppressive drugs are needed so that the cells are not rejected. Two patients in the study died, one from an infection linked to these drugs. Phase III studies are under way.
Sources: New England Journal of Medicine, June 2025 · HCPLive
A gene therapy designed for a single baby

In the US, a baby named KJ had a rare genetic disease (CPS1 deficiency) that causes ammonia to build up in the body. In about six months, researchers developed and delivered a personalised gene-editing treatment that corrected the baby's own mutation.
It is one of the first examples to show that making a treatment “tailored to each patient” is possible for very rare diseases.
Source: Innovative Genomics Institute, 2026
CRISPR treatments reach the clinic

Casgevy, the first approved CRISPR treatment, is used for sickle cell anaemia and beta thalassaemia. In studies, 16 out of 17 patients with sickle cell disease had no pain crises, and 25 out of 27 patients with thalassaemia did not need blood transfusions. Gene editing carried out directly inside the body is also showing promising results.
Thalassaemia and sickle cell anaemia are common in Turkey, especially in the Mediterranean region. The treatment is expensive and is not available at every centre.
Frequently asked questions
Can a blood test detect Alzheimer's?

Since May 2025, the US FDA has approved four tests that measure amyloid and tau changes in the brain from a blood sample. However, these tests are approved only for use in people with memory complaints, as part of an assessment by a doctor; they are not suitable for screening healthy people who have no symptoms.
Is trontinemab an approved Alzheimer's drug?

No, it is not yet approved; large phase III trials are ongoing. According to early-phase data, amyloid build-up in the brain fell below the threshold level at 28 weeks in 92% of patients who received the high dose. Side effects such as microbleeds in the brain were seen in a small number of patients.
Will AI read mammograms from now on?

No. In the MASAI study in Sweden, AI was used to support radiologists, not replace them. With this approach, more cancers were caught at screening, cancers found between screening rounds fell by 12%, and the false alarm rate did not rise.
Can pig organs be transplanted into people?

It is still experimental. A gene-edited pig kidney transplanted into a patient in the US kept him off dialysis for 271 days and then became a bridge to a human kidney transplant. The safety and durability of this approach are being studied in clinical trials.
Are GLP-1 weight-loss drugs now available as pills too?

Yes. In the US, oral semaglutide (the Wegovy pill) was approved in December 2025, followed in April 2026 by orforglipron (Foundayo), which can be taken with no food or water restrictions. In a 72-week study, average weight loss with the highest dose of orforglipron was 12.4%. These drugs are used together with diet and physical activity, under a doctor's supervision.
Are blood tests that catch cancer early ready for use?

Not yet. In the NHS-Galleri study of 142,942 people, the test picked up about 4 times as many cancers through screening and reduced stage IV diagnoses by 14%; however, the targeted reduction in stage III–IV cancers was not achieved, and its effect on survival is not yet known. These tests do not replace existing screening programmes.
Is there a stem cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease?

Not as a routine treatment yet. In an early-phase study called STEM-PD, dopamine cells made from stem cells were transplanted into 8 patients; of the 7 assessed after one year, 6 substantially reduced their medication dose, and no serious side effects were linked to the cells. Longer follow-up and larger studies are needed to see whether the effect lasts.
Does changing the way you walk reduce knee osteoarthritis pain?

In a study of 68 people, gait training with an individually chosen foot angle reduced pain by an average of 2.5 points out of 10 over one year; in the sham training group the reduction was 1.3 points. This is not a one-size-fits-all tip; it needs individual measurement and expert guidance.
Can exercise be part of cancer treatment?

In the CHALLENGE study of 889 people who had finished treatment for colon cancer, those who joined a 3-year, coach-supported exercise programme had a 28% lower risk of the cancer returning, a new cancer or death, and a 37% lower risk of death. Talk to your treatment team before starting an exercise programme.
Can thalassaemia and sickle cell anaemia be treated with gene therapy?

Casgevy, the first approved CRISPR treatment, is used for sickle cell anaemia and beta thalassaemia. In studies, 16 out of 17 patients with sickle cell disease had no pain crises, and 25 out of 27 patients with thalassaemia did not need blood transfusions. The treatment is expensive and is not available at every centre.

p.d: What causes low back pain, how long does it last and what do MRI findings mean? Six exercises to do at home, everyday tips, videos and warning signs.
s: The leading cause of disability worldwide. It may sound alarming, but most low back pain is not caused by a serious disease, and most new episodes of pain ease considerably within a few weeks. The key to recovery is movement, not rest.
619 million People worldwide living with low back pain (2020)
No. 1 Leading cause of disability worldwide
90%+ Low back pain with no identifiable structural cause
69% Recurrence within a year in people whose pain had cleared
What is it?

It is pain between the lower edge of the ribs and the crease of the buttocks. In more than 90% of cases of low back pain, no specific structural cause can be found; this is called non-specific or mechanical low back pain. The pain is real, but it does not mean that something in your back has "broken" or "slipped". Muscles, ligaments, joints and the nervous system's sensitivity to pain all play a part together.
If the pain spreads below the knee, into your leg and foot, with numbness or tingling, a nerve root may be affected: Lumbar disc herniation and sciatica →
What causes it?
Staying in the same position for a long time, especially sitting for hours
Heavy lifting you are not used to, sudden twisting or overexertion
Inactivity and weak trunk and hip muscles
Excess weight and smoking
Stress, anxiety, tiredness and lack of sleep
Physically demanding work
Work-related factors, smoking and high body weight account for about 39% of disability caused by low back pain, which means a large share of it can be prevented.
What do "flattening", "bulging" and "wear and tear" on an MRI mean?
The discs in your lower back change with age, much like hair turning grey. A review of the MRI scans of thousands of people with no back pain at all found:
52% Disc degeneration (wear and tear) at age 30
40% Disc bulging at age 30
80% Disc degeneration at age 50
60% Disc bulging at age 50

None of these people had low back pain. In other words, these phrases in an MRI report are often normal age-related changes and do not, on their own, explain the cause of pain. That is why guidelines do not recommend routine imaging for low back pain.
Course and treatment

When low back pain has just started, pain and limitation usually ease considerably within the first 6 weeks; in studies, pain scores fell by more than half on average. When pain lasts longer than three months, improvement is slower, and regular exercise and a guided treatment programme become even more important.
Staying active Bed rest is not recommended. Walking and carrying on with your daily activities as far as the pain allows speeds up recovery; if possible, avoid long periods off work.
Exercise The cornerstone of treatment. In long-lasting low back pain, exercise reduces pain by an average of 15 points on a 100-point scale. The best exercise is the one you can do regularly.
Manual therapy According to guidelines, mobilisation, manipulation and soft tissue techniques are beneficial when used together with exercise as part of a treatment package.
Coping with pain In long-lasting pain, fear, anxiety and poor sleep feed the pain. Cognitive behavioural approaches are recommended alongside exercise. Take a look at breathing exercises →
Medication Painkillers recommended by your doctor should be used at the lowest dose for the shortest possible time.
Not recommended Guidelines do not recommend back braces, insoles or traction.
Six key exercises for your lower back

Mild tension or discomfort is normal; if the pain settles back to its usual level soon after exercising, you have not done any harm. If the pain starts spreading into your leg or gets noticeably worse, stop that exercise. Start with the easier ones and build up over time.
Pelvic tilt
Pelvic tilt

Lie on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor. Gently tighten your stomach and press the hollow of your lower back down towards the floor; hold for 5 seconds, then relax. Do not hold your breath.
10 reps, twice a day
Knee to chest
Knee-to-chest stretch

Lie on your back. Hold one knee with both hands and slowly pull it towards your chest until you feel a gentle stretch in your lower back. If you like, gently lift your head towards your knee as you pull, keeping your shoulders on the floor (as in the Williams exercises); if you have neck pain, keep your head on the floor. Then repeat with the other leg.
Hold for 20–30 seconds, 3 times on each leg
Cat–camel
Cat–camel

Get down on your hands and knees. As you breathe out, round your back up like a cat and let your head drop. As you breathe in, slowly let your lower back sink and lift your head. Move slowly, within a pain-free range.
10 reps
Bridge
Bridge

Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Squeeze your buttocks and lift your back off the floor so that your shoulders, hips and knees form a straight line. Hold for 3–5 seconds, then lower slowly.
10–15 reps, 1–2 times a day
Bird dog
Bird dog

Get on your hands and knees with your back flat. Reach your right arm forwards and your left leg back, without letting your lower back arch or your hips rotate. Hold for 5 seconds, then repeat with your left arm and right leg.
8–10 reps on each side
Side plank on your knees
Side plank on your knees

Lie on your side, facing forwards, with your elbow directly under your shoulder, your forearm on the floor and your knees bent. Lift your hips off the floor so that your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. You can reach your top arm up towards the ceiling or rest your hand on your waist. Lower slowly, then turn onto your other side.
10–20 seconds, 3 times on each side
Looking after your back in daily life
Your back is much stronger than most people think, and it gets stronger with regular movement. Rather than being afraid of bending or lifting, it is better to get your body used to them gradually.
Get up every half an hour and walk a few steps; break up long periods of sitting.
Keep loads close to your body, take your time and do not twist while lifting.
Walk on most days of the week; short walks count too.
Look after your sleep routine; tiredness makes you more sensitive to pain.
Stopping smoking and losing excess weight are good for your back, too.
Exercise videos for low back pain
From the YouTube channel of US physical therapists Bob Schrupp and Brad Heineck.
Five exercises to ease low back pain
A short programme for new or recurring low back pain.
Five exercises for long-lasting low back pain
Strengthening and mobility exercises for low back pain that has lasted for months.
Frequently asked questions
Should I stay in bed and rest?

No. Guidelines recommend staying active. Resting for the first day or two when the pain is very bad is natural, but lying in bed for long periods weakens your muscles and slows recovery. Walk as much as the pain allows and carry on with your daily activities.
Should I wear a back brace?
Usually not. The UK guideline (NICE) for low back pain and sciatica does not recommend back braces, insoles or traction. Wearing a brace for a long time can make your muscles do less work.
Do I need an MRI scan?

Usually not. Disc degeneration and disc bulges are very common in people without any pain, too; finding something on an MRI does not mean that it is the cause of your pain. If there are warning signs or surgery is being considered, your doctor will decide.
Is a firm mattress better?

A very firm mattress is not essential. In a study of people with long-lasting low back pain, a medium-firm mattress gave better results than a firm one. The best mattress is one you sleep comfortably on and wake up from with less pain in the morning.
My pain has gone. Should I keep exercising?

Yes. Low back pain often comes back: in one study, 69% of people whose pain had gone had low back pain again within a year. Regular exercise and an active lifestyle are the best way to lower the risk of it coming back.
When to seek help right away
Low back pain is very rarely a sign of a serious disease. However, see a doctor without delay if you have any of the following:
Being unable to pass urine or to hold it in, or losing control of your bowels (emergency)
Numbness in the groin, around your bottom and in your inner thighs, i.e. loss of feeling in the "saddle area" (emergency)
Weakness or numbness in both legs at once, or loss of strength that keeps getting worse
Pain that starts after a fall or a blow, especially if you have osteoporosis
Pain together with fever, chills, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer
Severe night pain that keeps getting worse and does not ease with rest
Very severe low back pain that starts suddenly together with abdominal pain (call 112 )

p.d: Lumbar disc herniation and sciatica: symptoms, which nerve hurts where, does it heal on its own, when is surgery needed? Home exercises, videos and red flags.
s: It happens when a disc in the lower back bulges out and presses on a nerve root that runs to the leg. The pain shoots from the buttock down the leg, sometimes as far as the foot. The good news: most people recover without surgery, and the herniation often shrinks on its own.
95% Lumbar disc herniations found at the L4–L5 or L5–S1 level
70% Extruded herniations that shrink on their own
95% People with sciatica who feel recovered after one year
29% Disc herniation on MRI in 20-year-olds with no pain at all
What is it?

When the outer ring of a disc between the vertebrae weakens and tears, the gel-like core inside bulges out. The part that escapes presses on the nerve root running to the leg and causes inflammation there.
Sciatica is not the name of a disease but a symptom: pain spreading from the buttock down the leg along the sciatic nerve. Its most common cause is a lumbar disc herniation.
Symptoms
Pain spreading from the buttock into the leg, usually below the knee and into the foot; the leg pain is often worse than the back pain
Numbness, tingling or electric shock-like sensations in the leg or foot
Weakness in the foot or leg
Coughing, sneezing and sitting for a long time can make the pain worse
If the pain does not spread into your leg: Low back pain page →
Which nerve causes pain where?

Pain and numbness spread to different areas depending on which nerve root is compressed. Because 95% of lumbar disc herniations occur at the two lowest levels, the L5 and S1 roots are the most commonly affected.
L4 Pain and numbness Front of the knee, inner side of the leg Movements that may be weak Straightening the knee, pulling the foot up at the ankle
L5 Pain and numbness Outer side of the leg, top of the foot and big toe Movements that may be weak Lifting the big toe, walking on your heels
S1 Pain and numbness Back of the calf, heel, outer edge of the foot and little toe Movements that may be weak Walking on tiptoe
Diagnosis: when is an MRI needed?

The diagnosis is made first through a physical examination. The most important clues are leg pain brought on by raising your straight leg while you lie on your back (the straight leg raise test), along with checks of muscle strength, reflexes and sensation.

An MRI is needed if surgery or an injection is being considered, or if there are warning signs. Because disc herniations are also common in people without pain, MRI findings must always be interpreted together with your symptoms and examination.
Course and treatment

The natural course of a lumbar disc herniation is usually good. Over time, the body can clear away the disc material that has pushed out; the larger the herniation, the more likely it is to shrink. In a study comparing 283 patients who had had severe sciatica for 6–12 weeks, 39% of the group initially managed without surgery eventually had an operation; after one year, the results of the two groups were similar.
Staying active Bed rest is not recommended. Take short, frequent walks, avoiding positions that make the pain much worse.
Exercise Movements that draw the pain up from the leg towards the lower back, nerve gliding exercises and, over time, strengthening the back and hip muscles are the cornerstone of treatment.
Manual therapy Guidelines recommend manual therapy combined with exercise as part of a treatment package.

Medication and injections Painkillers recommended by your doctor. In acute, severe sciatica, an epidural injection targeting the nerve root may be given to selected patients if a doctor decides it is appropriate.

Surgery Considered if pain and limitation continue despite non-surgical treatment and the MRI findings match your symptoms. Loss of bladder or bowel control and worsening weakness, however, need emergency assessment.
Four exercises for sciatica

If the leg pain moves up towards your lower back during exercise, that is a good sign. If pain, numbness or tingling travels down the leg towards your foot, stop that exercise. For strengthening, you can also try the low back pain exercises .
90/90 rest position
90/90 rest position

When the pain is very severe, lie on your back and rest your calves on a chair or sofa, with your hips and knees bent at 90 degrees. This position reduces the load on your lower back and the nerve root.
10–15 minutes, if it brings relief
Prone press-up on elbows
Prone press-up on elbows

Lie on your front. Bring your elbows under your shoulders and slowly lift your chest off the floor, keeping your hips on the floor and your lower back relaxed. If the leg pain moves up towards your lower back, carry on; if it spreads down into your leg, stop.
10 reps, or hold for 1–2 minutes
Seated sciatic nerve glide
Seated sciatic nerve glide

Sit up straight near the front edge of a chair. As you straighten your knee, gently tilt your head back to look up at the ceiling. As you bend your knee, tilt your head forwards. The nerve is tightened at one end as it slackens at the other, so it glides without being stretched.
10 slow reps. Stop if the numbness increases
Bridge
Bridge

Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Squeeze your buttocks and lift your back off the floor so that your shoulders, hips and knees form a straight line. Hold for 3–5 seconds, then lower slowly.
10–15 reps, 1–2 times a day
Videos for sciatica and lumbar disc herniation
From the YouTube channel of US physical therapists Bob Schrupp and Brad Heineck.
Three safe exercises for sciatica
Safe movements to start with when pain spreads into your leg.
An exercise for sciatica, disc herniation and spinal stenosis
A key exercise for lumbar disc herniation and spinal stenosis, and how to do it correctly.
Frequently asked questions
Does a lumbar disc herniation go away on its own?

In most people, yes. Leg pain usually eases within weeks or a few months. What is more, the herniation can also shrink on MRI: it has been seen to regress on its own in about 70% of extruded herniations and in 96% of fragments that have broken away completely.
Do I need surgery?

Usually not. In a study comparing patients who had had sciatica for 6–12 weeks, early surgery relieved leg pain faster, but after one year the results of the two groups were similar, and 95% of patients in both groups felt they had recovered. Loss of bladder or bowel control and worsening weakness, however, may need emergency surgery.
Is it better to sit or to stand?
With a lumbar disc herniation, sitting for a long time makes the pain worse for most people. Keep sitting times short, and get up often to walk a few steps. Short, frequent walks usually help.
Can I do sport with a lumbar disc herniation?

Yes, as far as the pain allows. Starting with gentle activities such as walking and swimming, then moving on to exercises that strengthen your back and hip muscles, supports recovery. For a while, avoid movements that send the pain down your leg.
My MRI shows a disc herniation, but I have no pain. What should I do?

Don't worry. Even among 20-year-olds with no pain at all, about one in three have a disc herniation (protrusion) on MRI. If you have no symptoms, you do not need treatment; keep your back healthy with regular exercise.
When to seek help right away
The following signs may point to a condition called cauda equina syndrome, which can need emergency surgery, or to serious nerve damage. Go to an emergency department without delay:
Being unable to pass urine or to hold it in
Loss of bowel control
Numbness in the groin, around your bottom and in your inner thighs (the "saddle area")
New loss of sexual function
Sciatic pain, numbness or weakness in both legs at once
Being unable to lift your foot up (foot drop), or rapidly increasing weakness
Pain together with fever, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer

p.d: Why does neck pain happen, how long does it last, and does a straightened neck matter? Six exercises to do at home, desk tips, videos and warning signs.
s: Almost everyone has it at some point in their life. It is usually not caused by anything serious, but it often comes back. The good news: with regular movement and the right exercises, it can largely be kept under control.
203 million People worldwide living with neck pain (2020)
32% Expected increase by 2050
45–74 Most commonly affected age range
50–85% Pain returns within 1–5 years after a first episode
What is it?

Neck pain is pain anywhere from the base of the skull down to the shoulders. It usually comes from the muscles, the ligaments and the small joints between the vertebrae. Doctors call this mechanical or non-specific neck pain: the pain is real, but there is no serious disease behind it.

If the pain spreads into your arm and fingers with numbness, tingling or electric-shock sensations, a nerve root may be involved. We cover this on a separate page: Cervical disc herniation and pinched nerve →
What causes it?
Staying in the same position for hours: working at a desk, bending over your phone for long periods
Your neck being strained for a long time while you sleep, or a "crick" that comes on with a sudden movement
Stress, anxiety and poor sleep: they increase muscle tension and sensitivity to pain
Lack of activity and weak shoulder and upper back muscles
Age-related wear in the spine (osteoarthritis). Many people with no pain at all have this finding too.
Sudden whiplash-type injuries, such as in a traffic accident
Four types of neck pain
Physiotherapy guidelines divide neck pain into four groups. Treatment is shaped accordingly.
With limited movement
The familiar "crick in the neck". Your neck will not turn in some directions, and the pain gets worse when you move. This is the most common type.
With headache
Pain spreads from the neck to the back of the head, sometimes to the forehead, and is set off by neck movements. This is called cervicogenic headache.
With pain spreading into the arm
A nerve root is affected. There is pain, numbness, tingling or weakness in the arm.
With poor movement control
Mostly seen after a traffic accident. The neck muscles lose some of their coordination and endurance.
About a straightened neck and "bad posture"

Seeing "straightening of the neck" on an X-ray report worries many people. A study compared 107 people, 54 with neck pain and 53 without, and found no difference in neck curvature between the two groups. According to the researchers, findings like this are not the cause of the pain but incidental changes.

Posture is a similar story: there is no single "correct posture" for everyone. The best posture is the one you change often. The problem is usually not the position itself, but staying in the same position for too long.
Treatment
Most neck pain does not need an X-ray or MRI; the diagnosis is made through an examination. Treatment is planned according to the type of pain and how long it has lasted.
Staying active Bed rest and wearing a neck collar for long periods are not recommended. Carrying on with your daily activities as far as the pain allows speeds up recovery.

Exercise This is the cornerstone of treatment. Exercises that strengthen the neck, the shoulders and the muscles around the shoulder blades have been shown to reduce long-lasting neck pain moderately to markedly. Stretching exercises on their own may not be enough.
Manual therapy Mobilisation and manipulation of the neck and upper back, combined with exercise, improve pain and movement. They should be done by a trained physiotherapist after an examination.
Dry needling, TENS, laser Guidelines list these among the supportive options for long-lasting neck pain. They are worthwhile alongside exercise, not on their own.
Medication Painkillers recommended by your doctor can give short-term relief.
Stress and sleep When pain lasts a long time, managing stress and getting regular sleep are also part of treatment. Take a look at breathing exercises →
Six basic exercises for your neck
Do the exercises slowly and with control. A mild stretch is normal, but do not push into sharp pain. If the pain starts to spread into your arm, stop that exercise and talk to your physiotherapist.
Chin tuck
Chin tuck
Sit up straight, looking straight ahead. Without tilting your head, draw your chin straight back, as if making a double chin. Feel the back of your neck lengthen; hold for 5 seconds, then relax.
10 reps, 2–3 times a day
Neck rotation
Neck rotation
Keep your shoulders still. Slowly turn your head to the right and hold for 2–3 seconds at the furthest comfortable point, then turn to the left in the same way.
10 reps in each direction
Side stretch
Side stretch

With your right hand, hold the edge of the chair you are sitting on. Bring your left ear towards your left shoulder. You will feel a gentle stretch on the right side of your neck. Do not lift your shoulder.
Hold for 20–30 seconds, 3 times on each side
Shoulder blade squeeze
Shoulder blade squeeze
Stand or sit up straight. Without lifting your shoulders towards your ears, draw your shoulder blades back and slightly down towards each other. Hold for 5 seconds, then relax.
10–15 reps, twice a day
Isometric strengthening
Isometric strengthening
Place your palm on your forehead. Without moving your head, push gently into your hand while your hand pushes back. Repeat for the back and both sides of your head. Half your strength is enough.
5 seconds in each direction, 5 reps
Upper back (thoracic) extension
Upper back (thoracic) extension

Sit on a chair with a low back and clasp your hands behind your neck. Using the top of the backrest as a pivot, open your chest towards the ceiling and gently lean back. Stretch your upper back, not your neck.
5–10 reps
Looking after your neck at your desk
Hours spent in front of a screen are one of the most common triggers of neck pain. Small changes make a big difference.
Have the top edge of the screen at eye level or slightly below.
If you work on a laptop for long periods, use a laptop stand and a separate keyboard.
Raise your phone to eye level; lower your eyes, not your head.
Every half hour, get up, roll your shoulders and walk a few steps.
When you are on the phone, do not wedge it between your shoulder and your ear.
Exercise videos for neck pain
From the YouTube channel of US physical therapists Bob Schrupp and Brad Heineck.
The one neck exercise everyone should do
How to do the most basic neck pain exercise correctly.
Six exercises for a stiff neck
A short programme to get a stiff neck moving again.
Frequently asked questions
How long does neck pain last?

Most neck pain eases noticeably within days or a few weeks. However, it tends to come back: more than half of people who have it once get it again within 1–5 years. That is why it is important to keep up the exercises even after the pain has gone.
Should I use heat or cold?

For a stiff neck and muscle tension, gentle warmth helps most people. If you have had a recent knock or there is swelling, cold may be better in the first few days. Use whichever brings relief, for no more than 15–20 minutes, and protect your skin with a cloth.
Which pillow should I use?

There is no single best pillow for everyone. Choose a height that keeps your head level with your shoulder when you lie on your side, and does not push your head forwards when you lie on your back. Sleeping on your front can make the pain worse, because it keeps your neck turned to one side for a long time.
Should I wear a neck collar?
Not for ordinary neck pain. Wearing one for a long time can weaken the muscles and slow down recovery. After an accident, or when your doctor specifically recommends one, it is a different matter.
Do I need an X-ray or an MRI?

For most neck pain, no. Age-related wear and tear is common in people with no pain too, and often does not explain the pain. If you have one of the warning signs below, or the pain has not improved within a few weeks, your doctor will decide.
Is a straightened neck dangerous?
On its own, usually not. A reduced neck curve is common in people without pain too, and no link with pain has been shown. What matters are your symptoms and the examination findings.
When to seek help right away
Neck pain is usually harmless. However, see a doctor without delay if:
The pain started after a traffic accident, a fall or a blow
You have loss of strength in your arms or legs, clumsy hands (difficulty doing up buttons) or unsteadiness when walking
There has been a change in your bladder or bowel control
The pain comes with fever, chills, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer
You have severe night pain that keeps getting worse and does not ease with rest
You have a sudden, very severe headache, neck stiffness and a fever (call 112 )
You also have dizziness, double vision, or difficulty speaking or swallowing (call 112 )
Your neck pain comes with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating (it may be your heart; call 112 )

p.t: Cervical disc herniation and pinched nerve
p.d: Cervical disc herniation and pinched nerves causing arm pain: symptoms, which nerve goes where, what MRI shows, treatment without surgery, and when surgery is needed.
s: It happens when one of the discs in the neck bulges out, or when osteoarthritis in the spine pinches a nerve root. The pain shoots down into the arm and fingers, and there may be numbness and weakness. Most people recover without surgery.
83 New cases of a pinched nerve causing arm pain, per 100,000 people each year
4–6 months Time to clear improvement for most people
90% Have no symptoms, or only mild ones, in the long term
87.6% Disc bulges on the MRI scans of people with no pain at all
What is it?

Between the vertebrae are discs that act as cushions. When the outer ring of a disc weakens and tears, the gel-like core inside can push out; this is called a herniation. The part that pushes out presses on or irritates a nerve root that runs from the spinal cord to the arm.

A herniated disc is not the only cause of a pinched nerve causing arm pain (cervical radiculopathy). Especially in older people, a more common cause is bony spurs from osteoarthritis narrowing the opening where the nerve leaves the spine. In younger people, a herniated disc is more common.
Symptoms
Pain spreading from the neck to the shoulder, the shoulder blade and the arm, usually on one side
Numbness, tingling or electric-shock sensations in the arm, the hand or certain fingers
Weakness in the arm or hand, difficulty gripping
Tipping your head back or turning it towards the painful side may make the pain worse
Some people notice that their arm pain eases when they rest their hand on top of their head
If the pain is only in your neck and does not spread into your arm: Neck pain page →
Which nerve causes pain where?
Depending on which nerve root is pinched, pain and numbness spread to different areas. The root most often affected is C7, followed by C6.
C5 Pain and numbness Outer shoulder and upper arm Movement that may weaken Lifting the arm out to the side
C6 Pain and numbness Outer side of the forearm, thumb and index finger Movement that may weaken Bending the elbow, bending the wrist back
C7 Pain and numbness Middle finger Movement that may weaken Straightening the elbow, pushing
C8 Pain and numbness Ring and little fingers, inner edge of the hand Movement that may weaken Using the fingers, gripping
Diagnosis: MRI is not everything

The diagnosis is made first of all through an examination. A physiotherapist or doctor checks your neck movements, the strength of your arm muscles, your reflexes and your sensation. They also use special tests that load or relieve the nerve root, such as the Spurling test, the nerve tension test and the neck distraction test.

An MRI shows where the herniation is, but it cannot guide the decision on its own. Among 1,211 people with no symptoms at all, 87.6% had disc bulges on MRI; even in people in their 20s, the figure was 73–78%. What matters is whether the MRI findings match your symptoms and the examination.
Course and treatment

Symptoms are usually at their worst in the first few weeks. Most people improve clearly within 4–6 months, and this improvement still holds at 2–3 years of follow-up. In a study that followed 561 patients for about 5 years, 90% of patients had no symptoms or only mild symptoms at the final check-up; a quarter had had surgery.
Staying active It is enough to avoid, for a few days, the movements that make the pain much worse. Complete bed rest is not recommended.
Exercise Exercises that strengthen the deep neck muscles and the muscles around the shoulder blades and stabilise the neck, together with nerve gliding exercises, are the cornerstone of treatment.

Manual therapy and traction Guidelines recommend manual therapy and intermittent neck traction (a controlled pull on the neck), combined with exercise, for long-lasting pain that spreads into the arm.
Neck collar It can be worn for a short time in the first few days, when the pain is very severe. Long-term use is not recommended.
Medication and injections Painkillers recommended by your doctor. For selected patients, injections targeting the nerve root may be given if the doctor decides they are appropriate.

Surgery If there is progressive loss of strength, signs of spinal cord compression, or pain that disrupts daily life despite 6–12 weeks of appropriate treatment, an assessment by a neurosurgeon or an orthopaedic surgeon is needed.
Four exercises for a pinched nerve

If pain, numbness or tingling in your arm gets worse or spreads further down towards your fingers during an exercise, stop that exercise. If the pain draws back up from the arm towards the neck, that is usually a good sign. For strengthening and stretching exercises, see also the neck pain page .
Hand on head
Put your hand on your head

When your arm pain is severe, put the hand on your painful side on top of your head and rest like that. This position reduces the tension on the nerve root. For some people it eases arm pain considerably.
A few minutes, if it brings relief
Chin tuck
Chin tuck
Sit up straight, looking straight ahead. Without tilting your head, draw your chin straight back, as if making a double chin. Feel the back of your neck lengthen; hold for 5 seconds, then relax.
10 reps, 2–3 times a day
Nerve glide
Nerve glide

Raise your arms out to the sides at shoulder height, with your elbows bent to 90 degrees and your palms facing forwards. As you tilt your head to the right, straighten your right elbow and lower your forearm out to the side, so that your right arm is completely straight. Come back to the middle. Then tilt your head to the left and do the same with your left arm. The nerve is tightened at one end while it is slackened at the other, so it glides without being stretched.
10 slow reps to each side. Stop if the numbness increases
Shoulder blade squeeze
Shoulder blade squeeze
Stand or sit up straight. Without lifting your shoulders towards your ears, draw your shoulder blades back and slightly down towards each other. Hold for 5 seconds, then relax.
10–15 reps, twice a day
Videos for a pinched nerve in the neck
From the YouTube channel of US physical therapists Bob Schrupp and Brad Heineck.
Coping with a pinched nerve in the neck
A general roadmap of what can be done for pain that spreads into the arm.
The most important exercises for a pinched nerve
Key exercises for a pinched nerve and neck pain.
Frequently asked questions
Does a cervical disc herniation go away on its own?

For most people, yes. Symptoms are usually at their worst in the first few weeks, and most people improve clearly within 4–6 months. During this time, exercise and physiotherapy both reduce pain and make it easier to get back to daily life.
When is surgery needed?

A surgical assessment is needed if there is increasing weakness in the arm, signs of spinal cord compression such as clumsy hands and difficulty walking, or pain that disrupts daily life despite 6–12 weeks of appropriate treatment. In the long term, about a quarter of patients have surgery.
My MRI shows a herniated disc but I have no pain. What should I do?
Try not to worry. Most people with no pain have disc bulges on their MRI. If you have no symptoms, you do not need treatment; you can keep your neck healthy with regular exercise.
Is massage or neck "cracking" OK with a cervical disc herniation?

Soft tissue work and gentle mobilisation are generally safe. Fast, forceful neck manipulation ("cracking"), however, should only be considered when you have nerve symptoms spreading into your arm after a detailed examination, and by a trained practitioner.
How should I sleep?
Most people find it more comfortable to lie on their back or on their pain-free side. Your pillow should keep your neck in line with your spine. Avoid sleeping on your front.
Is a cervical disc herniation the same as a straightened neck?

No. A straightened neck means that the gentle natural curve of the neck looks reduced on an X-ray, and it is common in people with no pain too. A herniation, on the other hand, is a disc bulging out. About a straightened neck →
When to seek help right away
The following signs may mean that the spinal cord or nerves are seriously affected. See a doctor without delay:
Numbness or weakness in both arms at once
Clumsy hands: difficulty doing up buttons or writing, dropping things
Unsteadiness when walking, weakness or numbness in the legs
A change in bladder or bowel control (emergency)
Rapidly increasing weakness in the arm
Fever, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, or pain that started after an accident
Arm pain that comes with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating (it may be your heart; call 112 )

p.d: What is knee osteoarthritis, what does an X-ray show, and why do exercise and weight control matter? Six home exercises, daily tips, videos and warning signs.
s: A common knee problem, especially after the age of 45, that makes itself felt on stairs, when squatting and on long walks. Osteoarthritis does not mean "that's it, nothing can be done": with the right exercise and weight control, pain can ease considerably.
595 million People worldwide with osteoarthritis (2020); 7.6% of the population
75% Expected rise in knee osteoarthritis by 2050
1 kg → 4 kg Every kilo you lose takes about four times that amount of load off your knee with each step
12 points Average reduction in pain with exercise (out of 100)
What is it?

Osteoarthritis is a process that begins with thinning of the cartilage covering the joint surfaces, but it affects more than just the cartilage: the bone, the joint lining, the ligaments and the surrounding muscles are involved too. Bony outgrowths can form at the edges of the joint, and the joint may swell from time to time.

If you are over 45, with knee pain that gets worse with activity and morning stiffness that lasts less than 30 minutes, the diagnosis can usually be made from an examination; guidelines do not recommend routine imaging.
Symptoms and risk factors
Pain that gets worse going up and down stairs, when squatting or after walking for a long time
Brief stiffness in the morning or after sitting for a long time
Crackling in the knee, swelling from time to time, restricted movement
Risk factors: older age, being female, excess weight, previous knee injuries, jobs that put heavy strain on the knees, bow legs or knock knees
High body weight is responsible for about 20% of the disability caused by osteoarthritis.
Your X-ray and your pain do not always match

Being told "your X-ray looks really bad" often causes needless fear. In a review that pooled the research, only 15–76% of people with knee pain had osteoarthritis on their X-ray, while 15–81% of people with osteoarthritis on their X-ray had pain.

In other words, what your X-ray shows does not decide how bad your pain is or what you can do. What really matters is muscle strength, mobility, weight and daily activity. All of these can be changed.
Treatment
Guidelines put three things at the centre of treatment: exercise, weight control and understanding the condition properly.

Exercise This is the cornerstone of treatment. Exercise reduces pain by an average of 12 points out of 100 and makes everyday tasks easier. The programme includes movements that strengthen the thigh and hip muscles; a programme tailored to you and, if possible, started with the guidance of a specialist is recommended.

Weight control If you are overweight, any weight loss helps; losing 10% of your body weight is more effective than losing 5%. Every kilo you lose takes about four times that amount of load off your knee with each step.
Walking aids A walking stick or walking frame helps you stay mobile and independent during painful spells. Hold the stick in the hand on your pain-free side.
Medication Pain-relief gels rubbed onto the knee are the first choice. Painkillers taken by mouth should be used on your doctor's advice, at the lowest dose and for a short time only.
Cortisone injection into the joint When other treatments are not enough, it can give short-term relief lasting 2–10 weeks; your doctor decides whether it is right for you.
Joint replacement surgery This is considered if pain and restricted movement seriously affect your quality of life despite non-surgical treatment.

Not recommended in the guidelines: glucosamine supplements, hyaluronic acid injections into the joint, and arthroscopic "washing out" or "cleaning" of the knee (except in special cases such as a locking knee).
Six key exercises for the knee

You may feel some mild pain during exercise; if the pain is no worse the next day, it is safe to carry on. If there is a clear increase in pain, or swelling, the next day, cut down the number of reps. The first three are done lying down or sitting, so they are also suitable during painful spells.
Seated knee extension
Seated knee extension
Sit up straight on a chair. Slowly straighten one knee and lift your leg until it is parallel to the floor, tightening the muscle at the front of your thigh. Hold for 5 seconds, then lower slowly.
10 reps on each leg, twice a day
Towel press
Towel press

Lie on your back or sit with your leg stretched out, and place a rolled-up towel under your knee. Press the back of your knee down into the towel; the muscle at the front of your thigh will tighten and your heel will lift slightly. Hold for 5 seconds.
10 reps, 2–3 times a day
Straight leg raise
Straight leg raise
Lie on your back and bend one knee. Keeping the other knee straight and tightening your thigh, lift that leg up to the level of your bent knee. Lower it slowly.
10 reps on each leg
Sit-to-stand from a chair
Sit-to-stand from a chair
Cross your arms over your chest. Lean slightly forward and stand up from the chair, then sit back down with control. If it is hard, push up with your hands or use a higher chair.
10 reps, 1–2 times a day
Side-lying leg raise
Side-lying leg raise
Lie on your side with the bottom knee slightly bent. Lift the top leg with the knee straight and toes pointing forwards. Your hip muscles help keep the knee stable.
10–15 reps on each side
Half squat against the wall
Half squat against the wall

Lean your back against a wall with your feet half a step out from it. Let your back slide down the wall as you bend your knees slightly, going only as low as you can without pain, then straighten up. Do not let your knees go past your toes.
10 reps
Looking after your knees in daily life
Protecting your knee does not mean keeping it still; it means spreading the load wisely.
Walk on most days of the week; if the pain increases, walk for shorter periods but more often.
Cycling and exercising in water are good options that put less load on the knee.
Choose comfortable shoes with soft soles.
If squatting for a long time or getting down onto and up from the floor makes the pain worse, use a low stool or a chair instead.
After sitting for a long time, bend and straighten your knees a few times before you stand up.
Videos for knee osteoarthritis
From the YouTube channel of US physical therapists Bob Schrupp and Brad Heineck.
Seven exercises for knee osteoarthritis
A programme of strengthening and mobility exercises for a knee with osteoarthritis.
Non-surgical treatment for knee osteoarthritis
Approaches worth trying before surgery, and tips for everyday life.
Frequently asked questions
Should I rest my knee if it has osteoarthritis?

Long periods of rest are not recommended. Joint cartilage is nourished by movement; regular walking and strengthening exercises reduce pain and protect the knee. On days when the pain is much worse, ease off, but do not stop completely.
How should I go up and down stairs?
Hold on to the handrail. Going up, step up first with your good leg; coming down, step down first with your painful leg. If you use a walking stick, move it together with your painful leg.
Which hand should hold the walking stick?
In the hand on the opposite side to your painful knee. The stick touches the ground at the same time as your painful leg and reduces the load the knee has to carry.
Do glucosamine, collagen or knee injections work?

The UK guideline on osteoarthritis (NICE) does not recommend glucosamine supplements or hyaluronic acid injections into the joint. A cortisone injection into the joint, on the other hand, may be considered for short-term relief lasting 2–10 weeks when other treatments are not enough.
When is a knee replacement needed?

If pain and restricted movement seriously disrupt your daily life despite exercise, weight control and medication, you need an orthopaedic assessment. The decision is based on your quality of life, not on how your X-ray looks. Exercises done before and after surgery speed up recovery.
When to seek help right away
The following may point to a problem other than osteoarthritis. See a doctor without delay:
Sudden swelling, redness and warmth in the knee with a fever (possible joint infection)
Being unable to put weight on the leg after a fall or a twisting injury
The knee locking: it gets stuck and will not bend or straighten
Swelling, pain and redness in the calf (possible blood clot)
Night pain that does not ease with rest, or unexplained weight loss

p.d: What is frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis), who gets it, its stages, treatment options, exercises you can do at home, and videos.
s: A condition in which the shoulder first becomes painful and then gradually seizes up. It usually gets better on its own, but this can take months or even years. With the right exercise and treatment, you can get through this period more comfortably.
2–5% Prevalence in the general population
40–60 Most common age range
3–10 times More common in people with diabetes
1–3 years Typical duration of the condition
What is it?

The connective tissue that surrounds the shoulder joint, called the capsule, thickens, becomes inflamed and shrinks. The space for movement inside the joint narrows. The result: pain, and a clear restriction in lifting the arm, reaching behind you and turning the arm outwards.

Turning the arm outwards is usually the most restricted movement. Brushing your hair, putting on a jacket and fastening a clasp or belt behind your back become difficult. The pain is often worse at night, and lying on that side becomes difficult.
Who gets it?
People aged 40–60; more common in women
Much more common, and longer-lasting, in people with diabetes
Thyroid disease (an underactive or overactive thyroid)
Keeping the arm still for a long time after surgery, a fracture or an injury
Stroke, Parkinson's disease and heart disease
Some people who have had it in one shoulder may develop it in the other shoulder over the years.
Three stages
How long each stage lasts varies from person to person; it is usually longer in people with diabetes.
Painful stage
Pain gradually increases, especially at night. Range of movement starts to decrease.
Stiffening stage
Pain may ease, but the shoulder becomes very stiff. Everyday tasks are hardest during this stage.
Recovery stage
Movement slowly returns. Some people may be left with mild restriction for a long time.
Diagnosis and treatment

The diagnosis is usually made from an examination: the shoulder is equally restricted whether you lift your arm yourself or someone else lifts it for you. An X-ray, ultrasound or MRI is not needed to make the diagnosis, but one may be requested to rule out other causes such as osteoarthritis or a tear.

Physiotherapy and exercise This is the foundation of treatment. In the painful stage, the focus is on gentle movements within the pain-free range; in the stiffening stage, it moves to stretching and joint mobilisation. Regular exercise at home is very important.
Pain control Heat and painkillers recommended by your doctor make it possible to exercise.

Cortisone injection into the joint It can clearly reduce pain within a few weeks, especially in the early, painful stage. Its effect is mostly short-term; whether to have one is your doctor's decision.
