If you have knee pain, stay in a higher position; stop if the pain gets worse.
Do not stop or reduce your blood pressure medication on your own; exercise is added alongside your treatment.
Frequently asked questions
How can an exercise without movement lower blood pressure?

The mechanism is not fully understood. In a study done at home, the fall in blood pressure was mostly linked to a drop in resting heart rate and in the amount of blood the heart pumps each minute. Researchers are also looking at how blood vessels that are squeezed during the contraction and then widen when you release it may affect vascular health.
I take blood pressure medication. Can I do it?

Most people can, but talk to your doctor first and do not stop or reduce your medication on your own. Exercise is added alongside treatment, not instead of it. Measure your blood pressure regularly at home and share the results with your doctor.
Should I stop walking and just do wall sits?

No. In the analysis, all types of exercise lowered blood pressure. Aerobic exercise such as walking also matters for your heart, weight, blood sugar and mental health. Wall sits are a short, effective addition to your weekly activity.
How soon will I see an effect?
In small studies done at home, average falls of between 4 and 9 mmHg in systolic blood pressure were measured at the end of a 4-week programme. To keep the effect, you need to keep exercising.

p.d: The breathing technique that lifted mood more than meditation in a Stanford study: cyclic sighing. Breathe in twice, out long; do it with the 5-minute guide.
s: In a study at Stanford University, people who did 5 minutes of “cyclic sighing” every day for a month saw a bigger improvement in mood than people who spent the same time on mindfulness meditation. The method is very simple: breathe in twice through your nose, then take a long, slow breath out through your mouth. Follow along with the guide below.
5 min Daily practice time; the study lasted 28 days
108 people Participants randomly assigned to one of four methods: three breathing techniques and meditation
1.91 / 1.22 Average daily increase in positive emotions (points): breathing exercises vs meditation
Every few minutes How often we sigh on our own, without noticing
Breathing guide

Sit or lie down somewhere comfortable. As the circle grows, breathe in through your nose; when you feel full, add one more short breath in. As the circle shrinks, breathe out slowly through your mouth.
Start when you’re ready
Two breaths in through your nose, one long breath out through your mouth.
Duration
Pace
If you feel dizzy, go back to your normal breathing. If the pace doesn’t suit you, change it; what matters is that your breath out is longer than your breath in.
What did the research find?

In the Stanford study, 108 people practised one of four methods for 5 minutes a day for a month: cyclic sighing, box breathing, rapid breathing with breath holds, or mindfulness meditation. Participants rated their emotions before and after each session, and a device on their wrist measured their breathing rate and heart rate.
The daily increase in positive emotions was greater in the breathing groups than with meditation; the effect was clearest with cyclic sighing.
In people who practised regularly, the benefit grew over time.
Resting breathing rate fell in the breathing groups, especially with cyclic sighing; no similar change was seen with meditation.
Anxiety fell in all groups, with no difference between them.
Why breathe in twice?

Sighing is the body’s own tool: without noticing, we sigh on our own every few minutes. These deep breaths reopen the tiny air sacs in the lungs that have deflated. In cyclic sighing, you repeat this natural reflex on purpose.
Breathe in through your nose
Breathe in slowly until your lungs feel comfortably full.
Once more
At the point where you feel full, add a short second breath in; it can be a small one.
Take a long breath out
Breathe out slowly through your mouth until all the air is out. Let your breath out last longer than your breath in.
5 minutes
Repeat for 5 minutes every day. A few rounds can also help in a tense moment.
For more breathing exercises and skills for coping with stress, see What can you do in stressful moments? ; if you have trouble falling asleep, see For a good night’s sleep .
The physiological sigh
A short, widely watched video in which Stanford neuroscientist Andrew Huberman, one of the study’s authors, explains how to do the sigh and why it works.
Reduce anxiety and stress with the physiological sigh
Explains what breathing in twice and breathing out long does in the body.
Frequently asked questions
What time of day should I do it?

In the study, participants did it at whatever time of day they chose. Pick a time that can become a habit: before your morning coffee, at lunchtime or before bed. You can also do a few rounds in a tense moment.
Is it better than meditation?

In this study, the increase in positive emotions and the drop in breathing rate were clearer with cyclic sighing, while anxiety fell by a similar amount in all groups. This is a single study, and meditation remains a useful method too. Choose whatever works for you.
What should I do if I feel dizzy?

Go back to your normal breathing straight away. Don’t force your breath; the second breath in can be short and light. If you have a lung condition such as asthma or COPD, do it at a pace that feels comfortable.
How is it different from the breathing exercises on the stress page?

The stressful moments page covers 4-6, box and 4-7-8 breathing. What sets cyclic sighing apart is two breaths in, one straight after the other, followed by one long breath out. All of them rely on lengthening the breath out; choose whichever you find most comfortable.

p.d: People who spend 120 minutes a week in nature report better health. Your nature planner, places to go in Istanbul, awe walks and the power of a window view.
s: In a study of about 20,000 people in England, those who spent at least 2 hours a week in nature reported noticeably better health and wellbeing. It made no difference whether those 2 hours came in one go or in several shorter visits. In Istanbul, nature is closer than you think: a park, a grove, the shore or the seaside all count.
120 min Weekly threshold: below this, no clear difference was seen (19,806 people)
1.59 Odds ratio for reporting good health with 120–179 minutes a week in nature, compared with none
200–300 min The range where the benefit was greatest; no further benefit was seen beyond it
20–30 min Length of nature break at which the stress hormone cortisol fell most efficiently
Nature planner
Enter the time you have spent, or plan to spend, in nature this week. The planner is saved on this device and resets every Monday.
The thin green line on the ring marks 120 minutes; the full ring represents 300 minutes.
Where to this week?
You don’t need to go far; the park closest to your home counts too. A few suggestions:
European side
Belgrad Forest
Emirgan Grove
Yıldız Park
Maçka Park
Gülhane Park
Atatürk Urban Forest
Bebek–Rumelihisarı waterfront
Florya seafront
Asian side
Validebağ Grove
Fenerbahçe Park
Göztepe 60th Anniversary Park
Moda seafront
Büyük Çamlıca Hill
Kuzguncuk–Beylerbeyi waterfront
Polonezköy
Princes’ Islands
Even seeing trees from a window

In a famous study published in Science in 1984, researchers looked at the records of patients who had had gallbladder surgery. They compared 23 patients whose window looked out on trees with 23 similar patients whose window faced a brick wall.
Those who could see trees stayed in hospital for less time: 7.96 days on average versus 8.70 days.
They needed fewer strong painkillers.
Nurses’ notes contained fewer negative comments about them.
It was a small study, but it inspired hospital designers to make room for nature.
The awe walk

52 healthy older adults took a 15-minute walk once a week for 8 weeks. In the group asked to pay attention to a feeling of “awe” as they walked (that sense of wonder in the face of something far bigger than yourself), daily distress fell and emotions such as compassion and gratitude increased. In the photos they took on their walks, they gradually gave less space to themselves and more to the scenery, and their smiles became more noticeable.
Put your phone in your pocket
Taking photos is fine, but don’t walk along staring at the screen.
Notice what is vast
The breadth of the sea, the sky, the trunk of an old plane tree: look at things bigger than you.
See the small things too
The veins of a leaf, the moss between the stones, the flight of the gulls.
Something new each time
Choose a different route or time of day; even familiar places can surprise you with new details.
Frequently asked questions
Do I have to go to a forest or the countryside?
No. In the research, visits to open green and blue spaces such as city parks, groves, beaches and the countryside were all counted together. The park in your neighbourhood or the seafront works too.
Do I need to exercise?

No. Sitting or walking slowly in nature counts too. In the study that measured the stress hormone, participants were specifically asked not to do brisk exercise or use their phones. If you do walk, you get the benefits of movement as well.
Do I have to do the 120 minutes all at once?
No need. In the research, it made no difference whether the weekly time was made up of one long visit or several short ones. For example, 30 minutes on 4 days works too.
I can’t leave the house. What can I do?

Even seeing greenery from a window has been linked to better recovery. Open the curtains, sit near a window if you can, and grow plants on your balcony or windowsill. If you find it hard to get out of the house, physiotherapy can help you walk with confidence again.

p.t: Social connection: the forgotten health advice
p.d: People with strong social relationships are 50% more likely to survive. How loneliness affects health, surprising research and a small daily idea for connecting.
s: According to the World Health Organization, 1 in 6 people worldwide experience loneliness, and loneliness is linked to around 100 deaths every hour. In an analysis combining 148 studies, people with strong social relationships were 50% more likely to survive. The good news: connecting with others doesn't take big steps, and we tend to underestimate the effect of small ones.
1 in 6 People worldwide who experience loneliness (WHO, 2025)
871,000 Deaths linked to loneliness each year: about 100 every hour
50% Higher likelihood of survival in people with strong social relationships (148 studies, 308,849 people)
2× Likelihood of developing depression in people who feel lonely
Today's connection idea
One small step each day. If you don't like the idea, ask for another one; mark it when you've done it. Your weekly count is stored on this device and resets every Monday.
Send a short “thinking of you” message to someone you haven't spoken to in a long time.
Steps you've taken this week
Our predictions are wrong
Psychology research shows that we often avoid connecting with others because of mistaken predictions.
Talking to a stranger

When train passengers were asked to talk to the person next to them, they had a more enjoyable journey than those who kept to themselves, even though they had expected the opposite. The people they talked to enjoyed it too.
Thank-you letter
Writers underestimated how surprised and pleased the recipient would be, and overestimated how awkward the recipient would feel.
“Thinking of you”
About 6,000 people across 13 experiments: we tended to underestimate how much a short message or a small gift would be appreciated. When it was unexpected, the effect was even greater.
Voice call
People thought talking on the phone would be awkward; in fact, a voice call created a stronger sense of connection than messaging and took about the same amount of time.

The power of hugs: In a study in which 404 healthy adults were interviewed every evening for 14 days and then exposed to a common cold virus, those with strong social support and those who hugged more often were slightly better protected against infection; those who did fall ill also had milder symptoms.
Loneliness or being alone?
Loneliness
The painful feeling that comes from the gap between the relationships you want and the ones you have. You can feel lonely even in a crowd.
Social isolation
Objectively having few relationships and little contact. It may affect 1 in 3 older people and 1 in 4 adolescents.

According to the World Health Organization's 2025 report, loneliness and social isolation increase the risk of stroke, heart disease, diabetes, cognitive decline and early death. In the analysis of 148 studies, the effect of social relationships on the risk of death was comparable to that of well-known risk factors such as smoking and alcohol, and greater than the effect of physical inactivity and obesity.
For loved ones who can't leave the house
A stroke, a hip fracture, Parkinson's disease or long-lasting pain can leave a person isolated by confining them to their home and their bed. Loss of mobility and loneliness feed each other.
Visit or call regularly, and don't keep the conversation only to health.
Include them in family decisions and everyday tasks; feeling needed matters.
Hearing or vision problems can lead to withdrawal from social life; get them checked.
Walking confidently again also makes it easier to go out and meet people. See the guides to recovery after a stroke and after a hip fracture .
What makes a good life?
One of the most-watched TED talks in the world, by psychiatrist Robert Waldinger, director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has been running since 1938.
Lessons from the longest study on happiness
The key message of the study, which has followed hundreds of people from their youth into old age: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.
Frequently asked questions
Is it living alone or feeling lonely that's harmful?

Both. Social isolation (few relationships and little contact) and feeling lonely are different things, and both increase health risks. In the analysis of 148 studies, the link with survival was even stronger in studies that measured social relationships in more than one way.
Is messaging enough?

Messaging builds connection too, but in one study people who talked to old friends on the phone reported feeling more connected than those who wrote to them by email, and, contrary to what they expected, they didn't experience any more awkwardness. If you can, try a voice call or meeting face to face.
How many friends should I have?

There is no set number. As Robert Waldinger, director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has been running since 1938, stresses, what matters is the quality of your relationships more than their number: even a few close relationships you can trust are very valuable.
I've felt lonely and unhappy for a long time. What should I do?

This feeling is common and it can change. Small steps can help; but if you've had low mood, hopelessness or changes in sleep and appetite for weeks, see a doctor or a mental health professional. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call 112.

p.t: The DOST break: five minutes of being a friend to yourself
p.d: Four steps to treat yourself like a friend on a hard day: stop and name it, drop your shoulders, speak kindly, say thank you. A guided five-minute break.
s: If your closest friend were having a hard day, what would you say to them? Most likely something far gentler than what you say to yourself on the same kind of day. The DOST break turns that voice towards you for five minutes. “Dost” is Turkish for a true friend, and its letters name the four steps: D ur (stop), O muzlarını bırak (drop your shoulders), S eslen (speak to yourself), T eşekkür et (say thank you). By the end you will have written yourself a short note.
5 min Total time for the four steps; all you need is a quiet corner
20 s How long the soothing touch lasted in a study where it lowered the stress-hormone response
7 days How long people wrote to themselves as a friend would; the lift in mood was followed for months
27 trials A review of randomised controlled trials testing self-compassion practices
A five-minute break
Silence your phone and sit somewhere comfortable. There is no rush; stay with each step for as long as you like.
Dur: stop and name it
Pause for a moment. Which of these is most present in you right now? There is no right or wrong answer; pick the one that feels closest.
You don’t have to do the four steps in order. Even the 20-second touch is a break in its own right.
Why these four steps?
Each step rests on a small practice that has been studied on its own. We have written what was found, along with what was not.
Dur: stop and name it

When you are inside a feeling, everything blurs together. Giving it a name puts a little distance between you and it. In a brain-imaging study, when 30 people chose a word for the emotion while looking at angry and frightened faces, the brain’s alarm centre (the amygdala) was less active.
Omuzlarını bırak: drop your shoulders

Touch is the body’s oldest language of comfort. In a study of 159 people put through a stressful test, those who placed their hands on their heart and belly for 20 seconds had lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol than those who did not. Heart rate and how stressed they felt did not differ.
Seslen: speak to yourself

When we talk to ourselves, we are often our own harshest critic. Across seven studies with 585 people in total, those who addressed themselves by name rather than as “I” felt less distress in stressful situations. And people who wrote to themselves as a friend would for seven days were less depressed three months later and happier six months later.
Teşekkür et: say thank you

We tend to notice our body only when it hurts or in the mirror. In a study of 81 young women who were unhappy with their bodies, those who wrote about what their body can do became more satisfied with it, and the effect was still there a week later.
Let’s be plain

The DOST break is not a treatment; it is five minutes you set aside for yourself. Each of the four steps has been studied separately, but combined in this order they have not been tested as a whole. The sequence was put together for this site.

In a review of 27 randomised controlled trials testing self-compassion practices, stress, depression and anxiety improved to a moderate degree. The authors also note that the trials differed widely from one another and that positive results may have been more likely to be published.
When does it help?
On an evening when the pain is worse and you are about to get angry with your body.
On a day you skipped your exercises and have started blaming yourself.
Straight after hard news or a hurtful conversation.
Before sleep, as you close the day.
If you’d like to calm the body first, see The 5-minute cyclic sighing breath ; if you’d like to reach out to someone else, see Social connection and health .
Frequently asked questions
Isn’t this just self-pity?

No. Self-pity says “why always me” and leaves you isolated. Self-compassion says “this is hard, and I’m not the only one who struggles”. The aim is not to fool yourself or dodge responsibility; it is to be as fair to yourself as you would be to a friend you love.
Putting my hand on my heart feels odd. What should I do?

That’s perfectly natural. In the study, participants chose the touch that suited them; nearly all placed one hand on the heart and the other on the belly. You could cross your arms and hold your shoulders, or rest one hand inside the other. It can be done without anyone noticing, even on the bus.
How often should I do it?
There’s no rule. In the letter study, participants wrote on seven days in a row; you could try it for a week and see how you feel. A single round straight after a hard moment is fine too.
What if I feel worse while doing it?

When you start being gentle with yourself, feelings you have put off for a long time may come to the surface. Shorten the break, do only the touch step, or pause. If the distress continues, don’t carry it alone; talk to a mental health professional.

p.d: The 2026 Nobel Prizes in plain language: optogenetics, which switches brain cells on with light; the chemistry of one-handed molecules; and cosmic neutrinos caught in the ice of the South Pole. With animations, and a look at yesterday and tomorrow.
s: This year’s Nobel Prizes went to three questions: Can we talk to a single cell in the brain? Why does life always use just one hand? Can we get news from the far side of the universe? I have tried to explain all three simply enough to read over a cup of tea.
A door opened by light
Karl Deisseroth · Peter Hegemann · Georg Nagel
“for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”
In one sentence: A protein that lets a pond alga sense light was placed into brain cells; we can now switch chosen cells on and off with light, with a precision of one thousandth of a second.
Brain cells talk to each other with tiny electrical signals. In the cell’s membrane there are proteins that work like doors; when a door opens, charged particles rush in and the cell “fires”.
For years the problem was this: among billions of cells, how do we activate only the ones we want? An electrode stimulates every cell around it at once, and a drug is slow.

The answer came from a wholly unexpected place: a single-celled green alga living in pond water. This alga swims towards light because its membrane carries a door that opens when light touches it. Hegemann and Nagel found this door and showed how it works. Deisseroth and his team then placed its gene into nerve cells: the blue light came on, and the cell fired.
0 × fired
Above is the outside of the cell, below the inside. Blue light opens the door in the middle, charged particles rush in and the cell fires. Try it: one signal with every tap.
Yesterday 2002–2003: The alga’s light-gated doors (channelrhodopsins) were described. 2005: The door was placed into rat nerve cells; the cells fired within milliseconds of blue light.

Today Laboratories around the world use this method to map which circuits sleep, memory, fear, pain and movement run through. It is one of the key tools for understanding conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and depression at the level of circuits.

Tomorrow In 2021, a patient who had lost his sight to retinitis pigmentosa was able to notice, count and touch objects in front of him again, thanks to a light-gated door placed in his eye and a special pair of goggles. This was a single patient and the vision was partial; studies are continuing.

What it means for humanity: We no longer just watch the brain; we can ask it a question and get an answer. In Deisseroth’s words: “We’re not using light to collect information, we’re using light to cause things to happen.”
The hand in the mirror
Henri B. Kagan · Kenso Soai
“for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”
In one sentence: They showed how to make only one of two mirror-image molecules, and even how a tiny difference can amplify itself.

Look at your hands: they are mirror images of each other, yet a right-hand glove will not fit the left hand. Many molecules also come in two such forms, “right-handed” and “left-handed”. The same atoms, the same bonds; the only difference is the mirror image.

The body notices the difference at once: one hand of the same molecule smells of spearmint, the other of caraway. It is the same with medicines. More than half of the medicines we use are “handed” molecules like this, and often only one hand does the job.

Here is the strange part: in the laboratory, an ordinary reaction makes equal amounts of both hands. Living things, however, always use just one; the building blocks of our proteins are left-handed, and the sugars in our DNA are right-handed. How did this preference begin? The question had gone unanswered for more than a hundred years.
A right and a left mitten are mirror images, yet they do not sit on top of each other: the thumbs end up on opposite sides.
Kagan: The sleeping pairs

In 1986 Henri Kagan showed something surprising: even when the helper molecule that steers a reaction (the catalyst) was not completely pure, the product could come out almost pure. The reason is that the helpers go around in pairs; when a right and a left pair up, that pair falls asleep.
If three quarters of the helpers are right-handed and one quarter left-handed, the pairs are split like this:
56% right + right: at work
6% left + left: at work
38% right + left: asleep
Three quarters of the mixture was right-handed; nine out of ten of the pairs at work turned out right-handed.
Soai: A difference that multiplies itself

In 1995 Kenso Soai went a step further: he found a reaction in which the product helps to make copies of itself. If there is an excess of one hand at the start, too small to see, the difference grows with every round.
The two hands are almost equal. The excess of one hand is only 0.00005%.

Yesterday 1848: While sorting crystals one by one with tweezers, Louis Pasteur realised that molecules can come in two “hands”. 1986: Kagan showed the non-linear effect; 1995: Soai showed the reaction that multiplies itself.

Today Making only the right hand of medicine, scent and flavour molecules is now everyday work for the chemical industry. Kagan’s finding showed that a pure product can be obtained even with a helper that is not completely pure.

Tomorrow The question of why life chose one hand can now be studied by experiment: a tiny accident, through a reaction that multiplies itself, could turn into the preference of a whole world. This is an important clue about how life began; it is not a final answer.

What it means for humanity: That the medicine you take is of the right “hand” is the work of this chemistry. In the words of Heiner Linke, chair of the prize committee, the two scientists “have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously.” Henri Kagan received the prize at the age of 95.
A telescope inside the ice
Francis Halzen
“for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”
In one sentence: With a giant detector buried in the ice of the South Pole, he managed to catch “ghost” particles coming from the most violent events in the universe.

Neutrinos are particles that interact with almost nothing. Right now, trillions of them pass through your body every second and you feel nothing. They pass straight through stars, and even through the whole Earth, without stopping.
That makes them unique messengers: they set out from places light cannot escape and reach us in a straight line. For the same reason they are very hard to catch.

Halzen’s idea was this: very rarely, a neutrino does hit an atom and gives off a small flash of blue light. To see that light you need a medium that is very large, very clear and very dark. The ice of the South Pole is exactly that. Holes reaching about 2.5 kilometres down were melted into the ice with hot water, and thousands of light sensors were lowered into them. A cubic kilometre of ice became a telescope.

Above is the surface of the South Pole, below the strings of sensors deep in the ice. The neutrino arrives unseen and hits an atom; the sensors see the blue light of the resulting particle one after another, which gives away the direction it came from.

Yesterday 1930: Wolfgang Pauli predicted a particle that even he thought would never be caught. In 1956 the first neutrino was caught. In the late 1980s Halzen proposed turning the ice into a detector; IceCube was completed in 2011.

Today 2013: The first high-energy neutrinos from far beyond the Solar System were found. Then the sources began to appear: a giant black hole at the centre of a distant galaxy, the galaxy NGC 1068 and, in 2023, our own Milky Way.

Tomorrow A detector eight times larger (IceCube-Gen2) has been proposed. By reading light, gravitational waves and neutrinos together, the most violent events in the universe will be followed with different “senses”.

What it means for humanity: A completely new way of looking at the sky. For thousands of years we looked with light alone; now we can also read messengers that have travelled straight through matter. Halzen’s admission shows the human side of it: “Very few thought it would work, including myself.” After the prize he turned to his team of 450 scientists from 14 countries: “It’s a great relief for me to finally deliver the recognition that this great collaboration deserves.”
A curiosity that looked “useless”

How does a pond alga see light? Why does this reaction not add up? Would anything glow at the bottom of the ice? On the day they were asked, none of these three questions looked as if it would ever ease anyone’s troubles. Nobody started studying algae saying “I am going to treat blindness”.

The time in between is worth a thought too: more than twenty years passed from the discovery of the alga’s door to the prize, and forty years from Kagan’s finding. Science is mostly a marathon; the prize is the photograph taken at the finish line.

As a physiotherapist, the one closest to me is the door opened by light: part of the knowledge we lean on when rebuilding movement after a stroke or in Parkinson’s disease comes from the maps of brain circuits drawn with this method.
A small question asked with patience may one day touch the life of someone we have never met.
Frequently asked questions
What is optogenetics?
It is a method of placing a light-sensitive protein into nerve cells and switching them on and off with light. This lets researchers test directly what a particular group of cells in the brain does.
Is optogenetics used as a treatment in people?

It is not yet a routine treatment. In 2021, partial recovery of vision was reported in one patient who had lost his sight to retinitis pigmentosa; clinical studies are continuing. Today the method is used mainly in research laboratories.
What does it mean for a molecule to be “right-handed” or “left-handed”?

Some molecules, just like a right and a left hand, cannot be laid on top of their mirror image; this is called chirality. The two forms are made of the same atoms but can behave differently in the body. That is why obtaining the right form matters in making medicines.
What is a neutrino, and is it harmful?

A neutrino is a fundamental particle with no electric charge and a very small mass. Trillions of them pass through our bodies every second; because they hardly interact with matter at all, they do us no harm.
